blocks.text: By now you know what a deque is and how its operations work. The real question is: when should you actually reach for one?
A deque shines in a very specific situation: when a problem needs fast access to both ends of a moving range of data. That sounds narrow, but it shows up in some of the most loved interview problems.
If a problem talks about a window, a range, or the most recent items, a deque is often hiding inside the optimal solution.

content.title: 1. The Star Use Case: Sliding Window Maximum

blocks.text: This is the problem that makes deques famous. You are given an array and a window of size k that slides across it. For every position of the window, you must report the maximum value inside it.
The brute force way is to scan all k elements at every step, which is slow. A deque turns this into a single clean pass over the array.

The trick is to keep a monotonic deque, a deque whose values stay in decreasing order. We store array indices, and before adding a new element we remove from the back every element smaller than it, because those can never be the maximum again.
The front of the deque always holds the index of the current maximum. Each element is added and removed at most once, so the whole algorithm runs in O(n).
A deque that stays sorted as you push and pop is called a monotonic deque. It is the single most important deque pattern for interviews.
A breadth first search needs a queue, and a deque makes a perfect, efficient queue. You push newly discovered nodes to the back and pop the next node to visit from the front.
There is also a neat trick called 0 1 BFS. When edges have weights of only 0 or 1, you can find shortest paths using a deque instead of a slower priority queue:

items: For an edge with weight 0, push the neighbour to the front
For an edge with weight 1, push the neighbour to the back

blocks.text: This keeps the nodes ordered by distance automatically, which gives you shortest paths in linear time.
Beyond the famous problems, deques quietly power many smaller tasks:

items: Palindrome check: compare the front and back characters, then move inward.
Undo and redo: keep recent actions at one end and discard the oldest from the other.
Sliding window minimum or maximum: any problem tracking an extreme over a moving range.
Recent history with a limit: add new items at the back and drop old ones from the front when full.

blocks.text: Notice the common thread: every one of these needs quick access to the newest and the oldest item at the same time.

content.title: 4. How to Spot a Deque Problem

blocks.text: You will rarely be told to use a deque. You have to recognise the signals yourself:

items: A window of fixed or variable size slides across an array
You need the maximum or minimum of the current window quickly
You keep removing stale elements from one end while adding fresh ones at the other
A plain queue is close, but you also need to remove from the same end you just added to

blocks.text: When you see those clues, ask whether a monotonic deque can replace a slow inner loop. The answer is surprisingly often yes.
